knowledge_statements.title: Submodularity under Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submodularity of the L-convex conjugate produced from an M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper M-convex and suppose its integral conjugate \(g=f^{\bullet}\) is proper. Since \(g\) is L-convex, it is submodular on the integer lattice: for all \(p,q\in\mathbb Z^n\),
\[g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\wedge q)+g(p\vee q),\]
where the meet and join are taken componentwise. Thus M-convex exchange structure becomes lattice submodularity after integral conjugation; the accompanying L-convex translation law supplies the additional structure beyond submodularity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integral conjugate of an M-convex function is L-convex and therefore satisfies the componentwise lattice submodularity inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper integer-valued M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(p)+g(q)\ge g(p\wedge q)+g(p\vee q)\) for every \(p,q\in\mathbb Z^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: M–L Fenchel Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong integral Fenchel duality for an M-convex and an L-convex summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper M-convex and \(g:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper L-convex. Define integral conjugates by \(h^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-h(x)\}\). If \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\) and the primal minimum is finite and attained, then
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{f(x)+g(x)\}=\max_{p\in\mathbb Z^n}\{-f^{\bullet}(p)-g^{\bullet}(-p)\}.\]
Under the standard properness conditions for the dual functions, the maximum is attained by an integral dual vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compatible M-convex and L-convex functions, minimizing their sum over integer points equals an attained maximization involving their integral conjugates.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper integer-valued M-convex and \(g\) is proper integer-valued L-convex.
The primal value is finite and attained, with the dual conjugates proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x(f(x)+g(x))=\max_p(-f^{\bullet}(p)-g^{\bullet}(-p))\), with an integral dual maximizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrally Convex–Separable Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete Fenchel duality for an integrally convex function and a separable convex summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper integrally convex and let \(\Psi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_i(x_i)\), where every \(\psi_i:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper discrete convex. Define \(h^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-h(x)\}\). \[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{f(x)+\Psi(x)\}=\max_{p\in\mathbb Z^n}\{-f^{\bullet}(p)-\Psi^{\bullet}(-p)\}.\]
When the primal minimum is attained, an integral dual maximizer exists under the same qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Separation Theorems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict affine separation for disjoint finite M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be nonempty finite M-convex sets. If \(S\cap T=\varnothing\), then their integral base-polyhedral convex hulls are disjoint. Consequently, there exist \(p\in\mathbb Q^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\) such that
\[
\langle p,x\rangle<\alpha<\langle p,y\rangle
\quad(x\in S,\ y\in T).
\]
After multiplying by a common denominator, \(p\) and \(\alpha\) may be chosen integral while preserving strict separation after an appropriate rescaling of the gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two disjoint finite M-convex sets admit a strict rational affine separator, which can be rescaled to integral data.
assumptions_latex: \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) are nonempty finite M-convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(p,\alpha)\in\mathbb Q^n\times\mathbb Q\) with \(\langle p,x\rangle<\alpha<\langle p,y\rangle\) for all \(x\in S\), \(y\in T\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean pairing of the separating price vector and a lattice point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partition-quota SDR criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes SDRs whose representatives meet prescribed lower and upper counts in every partition class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\} be partitioned into P_1,\ldots,P_p, and let integers 0\leq a_k\leq a'_k be given. Subsets S_1,\ldots,S_n\subseteq E have an SDR R satisfying \(a_k\leq|R\cap P_k|\leq a'_k\) for every k if and only if, for all U\subseteq[p] and V\subseteq[n], \[\left|\left(\bigcup_{k\in U}P_k\right)\cap\left(\bigcup_{j\in V}S_j\right)\right|\geq \max\left\{|V|-\sum_{k\in U}a'_k,\ |V|-n+\sum_{k\in U}a_k\right\}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: General Discrete Lagrangian Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak Lagrange duality for equality-constrained lattice optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and consider \(v_P=\inf\{f(x)\mid x\in X,\ Ax=b\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). For \(p\in\mathbb R^m\), define
\[
L(x,p)=f(x)+\langle p,Ax-b\rangle,
\qquad q(p)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,p).
\]
The Lagrange dual value is \(v_D=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^m}q(p)\), and weak duality always gives \(v_D\le v_P\). Equality and dual attainment require additional discrete-convex regularity or an exact penalty/separation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing lattice equality constraints by prices produces a concave dual function whose supremum is always a lower bound on the primal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_D=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^m}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,p)\le v_P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-duality formulation is mathematically standard and the duality kind fits, but no cited source supports its placement as a discrete Lagrangian framework.

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Lagrangian Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of M-convexity under Lagrangian linear perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper M-convex function and impose \(Ax=b\). For every multiplier \(p\in\mathbb R^m\), define
\[
L_p(x)=f(x)+\langle A^{\mathsf T}p,x\rangle-\langle p,b\rangle.
\]
Then \(L_p\) is M-convex, because adding an affine function preserves the M-exchange inequality. Hence \(q(p)=\inf_xL_p(x)\) can be evaluated by M-convex minimization whenever its infimum is finite, and \(q\) is concave. Strong Lagrange duality is not asserted without an appropriate integral separation or constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every multiplier produces an M-convex subproblem; its minimum defines a concave dual function, while strong duality needs extra hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper M-convex function on \(\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_p\) is M-convex for every \(p\), and \(q(p)=\inf_xL_p(x)\) is concave.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Affine perturbation preserves M-convexity and the dual value is concave, but a precise source is needed for the M-convex formulation and its extended-real finiteness conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Primal–Dual Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate symmetry for a proper closed discrete-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed discrete-convex function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define its discrete conjugate on admissible price vectors by
\[
f^{\bullet}(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb Z^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\}.
\]
Whenever the selected M/L-convex conjugacy theorem applies, biconjugacy gives
\[
f(x)=\sup_p\{\langle p,x\rangle-f^{\bullet}(p)\}.
\]
Thus primal lattice points and dual prices enter symmetrically: \(p\in\partial f(x)\) if and only if \(x\in\partial f^{\bullet}(p)\), equivalently \(f(x)+f^{\bullet}(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete conjugacy exchanges lattice points and prices; equality in the conjugate inequality is equivalent to either mutual subgradient condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and closed in a discrete-convex class admitting biconjugacy.
\(x\) and \(p\) belong to the corresponding primal and price domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\partial f(x)\Longleftrightarrow x\in\partial f^{\bullet}(p)\Longleftrightarrow f(x)+f^{\bullet}(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Discrete conjugate of the primal function.
Discrete subdifferential at the primal point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends M- and L-convex conjugacy without fixing the function class, admissible price domain, or matching subdifferential definitions. An exact conjugacy theorem and locator are needed before the displayed equivalences can be assessed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange-Direction Optimality Criterion for M-Natural-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality using a dummy zero element to include single-coordinate moves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^{V}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be M^{\natural}-convex and x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Adjoin 0\notin V and define \chi_0=0\in\mathbb{R}^{V}. Then x is a minimizer of f if and only if f(x+\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v))\geq f(x) for every u,v\in V\cup\{0\} and every \alpha>0. If f is domain-integral and x\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}, the equivalence remains valid when the quantifier over \alpha>0 is replaced by \alpha=1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain point of an M-natural-convex function is globally minimizing exactly when no positive exchange or single-coordinate step decreases its value. For a domain-integral function at an integral point, the equivalent test requires only unit steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\iff(\forall u,v\in V\cup\{0\})(\forall\alpha>0)\ f(x+\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v))\geq f(x);\quad f\text{ domain-integral},\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\implies\left[x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\iff(\forall u,v\in V\cup\{0\})\ f(x+\chi_u-\chi_v)\geq f(x)\right]

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Steepest-Descent Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-exchange descent for finite-valued M-convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an M-convex function \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), at iteration \(k\) choose
\[
(i_k,j_k)\in\arg\min_{i,j}\ f(x^k-e_i+e_j)
\]
over feasible unit exchanges. If the minimum is at least \(f(x^k)\), stop and output \(x^k\); otherwise set \(x^{k+1}=x^k-e_{i_k}+e_{j_k}\). The M-exchange axiom implies that the stopping condition is equivalent to global optimality. With steepest choices, the number of iterations equals the minimum exchange distance from \(x^0\) to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly take the best feasible unit exchange. Absence of an improving exchange certifies global M-convex optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is M-convex and has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates at \(x^*\in\arg\min f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-exchange algorithm and local-optimality conclusion fit the leaf, but the exact iteration-count assertion depends on the definition of exchange distance and the applicable steepest-descent theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Scaling Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse-to-fine exchange minimization with proximity recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a power of two \(\alpha_0\) covering the relevant coordinate range and an initial feasible point \(x^{(0)}\). At scale \(\alpha\), minimize the restriction of \(f\) to the congruence lattice \(x^{(0)}+\alpha\mathbb Z^n\) by feasible exchanges \(x\mapsto x-\alpha e_i+\alpha e_j\). When no such exchange improves the objective, use the M-convex proximity theorem to restrict the next search to a certified neighborhood of the current point, replace \(\alpha\) by \(\alpha/2\), and repeat. At \(\alpha=1\), unit-exchange local optimality yields a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: M-convex scaling solves coarse congruence-lattice problems, halves the scale using proximity bounds, and finishes with exact unit-exchange optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is M-convex with nonempty bounded effective domain.
\(\alpha_0\) is a power of two large enough for the coordinate range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At the terminal scale \(\alpha=1\), the returned point belongs to \(\arg\min f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes the intended scaling family, but the congruence-lattice initialization, proximity neighborhood, and transition between scales are not precise enough without a cited algorithm and proximity theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steepest-Descent Scaling Algorithm for M-Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximity-based scaling method for an M-convex function with bounded effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be M-convex with bounded effective domain and K_\infty=\max\{\lVert p-q\rVert_\infty:p,q\in\operatorname{dom}f\}. Choose x\in\operatorname{dom}f, set \alpha=2^{\lceil\log_2(K_\infty/(4n))\rceil} and B=\operatorname{dom}f. At each scale, use steepest descent initialized at 0 to find an integer vector y locally minimizing \widetilde f(y)=f(x+\alpha y) when x+\alpha y\in B and +\infty otherwise, and set x\leftarrow x+\alpha y. If \alpha=1, return x. Otherwise set B\leftarrow B\cap\{z\in\mathbf{Z}^{V}:\lVert z-x\rVert_\infty\leq(n-1)(\alpha-1)\}, set \alpha\leftarrow\alpha/2, and repeat. The returned x is a minimizer of f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each scale, solve a rescaled restricted problem by exchange steepest descent, update the current point, restrict the retained domain to the prescribed proximity box, and halve the scale. At scale one, the current point is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha=1\Longrightarrow x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain-reduction scaling algorithm for M-convex minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling algorithm that maintains a domain point and a coordinatewise lower bound whose upper orthant contains a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be M-convex and $S(\ell)=\{y\in\mathbf Z^V\mid y\ge\ell\}$. Maintain $x\in S(\ell)\cap\operatorname{dom}f$ and $S(\ell)\cap\arg\min f\ne\varnothing$. Starting from $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, set $\ell=x-K_\infty\mathbf1$ and $\alpha=2^{\lceil\log_2(K_\infty/(2n))\rceil}$. During each $\alpha$-scaling phase, update $(x,\ell)$ by scaled exchanges and lower-bound increases until $\ell\le x\le\ell+(n-1)(\alpha-1)\mathbf1$. If $\alpha>1$, replace $\alpha$ by $\alpha/2$ and repeat. When $\alpha=1$, the bound gives $x=\ell$, and the maintained invariants imply $x\in\arg\min f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method combines domain reduction with halving-scale exchange phases. Each phase preserves a current domain point and an upper orthant containing a minimizer while tightening the coordinatewise gap. At scale one the current point equals the lower bound and is optimal.
assumptions_latex: K_\infty\text{ is as defined for the algorithm}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha=1\implies x=\ell\quad\text{and}\quad x\in\arg\min f

knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Domain-Reduction Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certified shrinking of a box containing an M-convex minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain an integral box \(B^k=[\ell^k,u^k]_{\mathbb Z}\) known to contain at least one minimizer of an M-convex function \(f\). Solve prescribed exchange or price-perturbed subproblems on \(B^k\) to obtain a valid certificate that some slab \(H^k\subset B^k\) contains no minimizer. Set \(B^{k+1}=B^k\setminus H^k\), represented by the certified smaller box, and continue until the remaining box is a singleton or direct exchange minimization is invoked. Correctness requires each reduction certificate to preserve
\[
B^{k+1}\cap\arg\min f\ne\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain-reduction methods repeatedly remove certified minimizer-free coordinate slabs while retaining at least one M-convex minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is M-convex and has a minimizer in the initial finite box \(B^0\).
Every reduction step supplies a valid minimizer-exclusion certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain-Reduction Algorithm for M-Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested-domain method based on central points, improving exchanges, and M-minimizer cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be M-convex with bounded effective domain. For a bounded nonempty set B\subseteq\mathbf{Z}^{V}, define \ell_B(v)=\min_{y\in B}y(v), u_B(v)=\max_{y\in B}y(v), \ell_B^{\circ}=\lfloor(1-1/n)\ell_B+(1/n)u_B\rfloor, u_B^{\circ}=\lceil(1/n)\ell_B+(1-1/n)u_B\rceil, and B^{\circ}=\{y\in B:\ell_B^{\circ}\leq y\leq u_B^{\circ}\}. Initialize B=\operatorname{dom}f. Choose x\in B^{\circ} and distinct u,v minimizing f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v). If f(x)\leq f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v), return x; otherwise set B\leftarrow B\cap\{y\in\mathbf{Z}^{V}:y(u)\leq x(u)-1,\ y(v)\geq x(v)+1\} and repeat. The returned x is a minimizer of f. Moreover, B^{\circ}\neq\varnothing when B is M-convex, and the algorithm runs in time polynomial in n and \log_2K_\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a nested subset of the bounded effective domain. Choose a point in its central region and test the best unit exchange. A nonimproving best exchange certifies global optimality; an improving exchange determines a coordinate cut before repetition. The central region is nonempty for an M-convex working set, and the method has polynomial running time in n and log K-infinity.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is bounded and nonempty when }B^{\circ}\text{ is formed}
B\text{ is M-convex for the assertion }B^{\circ}\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\leq f(x-\chi_u+\chi_v)\Longrightarrow x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f,\qquad T=\operatorname{poly}(n,\log_2K_\infty)

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Steepest-Descent Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood descent for L-natural-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be L-natural-convex and start from \(x^0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). At iteration \(k\), minimize \(f\) over
\[
N(x^k)=\bigl(x^k+\{0,1\}^n\bigr)\cup\bigl(x^k-\{0,1\}^n\bigr).
\]
If a minimizer \(y^k\in N(x^k)\) satisfies \(f(y^k)<f(x^k)\), set \(x^{k+1}=y^k\); otherwise stop. L-natural-convex local optimality implies that the output is globally minimizing. Each neighborhood subproblem is a submodular set-function minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize over the upward and downward unit cubes around the current point; no local improvement certifies global L-natural-convex optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is L-natural-convex and attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stopping point \(x^*\) satisfies \(x^*\in\arg\min f\).

notation.meaning: Union of the upward and downward Boolean neighborhoods of x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood-descent algorithm, global local-optimality criterion, and submodular neighborhood subproblems are standard for L-natural-convex functions, but no theorem or section citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Scaling Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse-to-fine neighborhood descent for L-natural-convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a power-of-two scale \(\alpha_0\). At scale \(\alpha\), apply steepest descent using the neighborhoods
\[
N_\alpha(x)=\bigl(x+\alpha\{0,1\}^n\bigr)\cup\bigl(x-\alpha\{0,1\}^n\bigr)
\]
until no improving point remains in \(N_\alpha(x)\). A proximity theorem for the scaled L-natural-convex objective supplies a bounded region containing a finer-scale minimizer. Restrict to that region, replace \(\alpha\) by \(\alpha/2\), and repeat. When \(\alpha=1\), neighborhood local optimality certifies a global minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled Boolean-neighborhood descent halves its step size under a proximity bound and becomes exact at unit scale.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is L-natural-convex and has a minimizer in a known bounded region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unit-scale terminal point lies in \(\arg\min f\).

notation.meaning: Scaled upward and downward Boolean neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steepest-Descent Scaling Algorithm for L-Convex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling algorithm for an L-convex function satisfying the source-referenced condition (10.31).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf R]\) satisfy (10.31), and define \(\widehat K_\infty=\max\{\|p-q\|_\infty\mid p,q\in\operatorname{dom}g,\ p(v)=q(v)\text{ for some }v\in V\}\). Choose \(p\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and set \(\alpha=2^{\lceil\log_2(\widehat K_\infty/(2n))\rceil}\). At each scale, apply steepest descent with initial vector \(0\) to find an integer vector \(q\) such that, for \(\widetilde g(q)=g(p+\alpha q)\), \(\widetilde g(q)\leq\widetilde g(q+\chi_X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\), and then set \(p\leftarrow p+\alpha q\). If \(\alpha=1\), stop and return \(p\), a minimizer of \(g\); otherwise set \(\alpha\leftarrow\alpha/2\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a domain point and initialize a power-of-two scale from the specified domain parameter. At each scale, run steepest descent from zero to obtain the stated local minimum of the scaled function, update the current point, and halve the scale. At scale one, the returned point is a global minimizer of the L-convex function.
assumptions_latex: g\in\mathcal L[\mathbf Z\to\mathbf R]\text{ satisfies the source-referenced condition (10.31)}
\widehat K_\infty=\max\{\|p-q\|_\infty\mid p,q\in\operatorname{dom}g,\ p(v)=q(v)\text{ for some }v\in V\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{When the algorithm reaches }\alpha=1,\quad p\in\operatorname*{argmin} g.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction to Submodular Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean-neighborhood subproblems represented as submodular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be L-natural-convex and fix \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Define set functions on \(2^{[n]}\) by
\[
h_x^+(S)=f(x+\mathbf 1_S),
\qquad h_x^-(S)=f(x-\mathbf 1_S).
\]
The discrete midpoint inequality implies that both \(h_x^+\) and \(h_x^-\) are submodular on their effective domains. Therefore minimizing \(f\) over the upward or downward Boolean neighborhood of \(x\) reduces exactly to submodular set-function minimization; comparing the two minima produces an L-natural-convex steepest-descent step or a local-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting an L-natural-convex function to either Boolean neighborhood yields a submodular set function, enabling exact local minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_x^+\) and \(h_x^-\) are submodular, and their minima equal the corresponding neighborhood minima of \(f\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of the subset S.
Upward and downward Boolean restrictions of f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Boolean-neighborhood representation is appropriate, but a precise source is required, particularly for the extended-valued meaning of submodularity and treatment of infeasible subsets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Local Optimality Under Diagonal Translation Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced global-minimum test for integrally convex functions invariant under translation by the all-ones vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be integrally convex and satisfy $f(z+\mathbf 1)=f(z)$ for every $z\in\mathbb Z^n$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbb Z}f$,
\[(\forall y\in\mathbb Z^n)\ f(x)\le f(y)\iff (\forall Y\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\})\ f(x)\le f(x+\chi_Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integrally convex function invariant under translation by the all-ones vector, a finite-valued lattice point is globally minimizing exactly when increasing any subset of its coordinates by one cannot improve the value.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is integrally convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall y\in\mathbb Z^n)\ f(x)\le f(y)\iff(\forall Y\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\})\ f(x)\le f(x+\chi_Y).

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimality Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cube optimality criterion for integrally convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be integrally convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then \(x\) is a global minimizer if and only if
\[
f(x)\le f(x+d)
\quad\text{for every }d\in\{-1,0,1\}^n.
\]
Values outside \(\operatorname{dom}f\) are interpreted as \(+\infty\). Thus exhaustive comparison on the integral unit neighborhood is a complete optimality test, although the neighborhood may contain exponentially many points in the dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integrally convex function, a lattice point is globally optimal exactly when no point in its unit cube has smaller value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\arg\min f\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\le f(x+d)\) for all \(d\in\{-1,0,1\}^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-neighborhood condition is an appropriate local-optimality criterion for integrally convex functions, but the candidate supplies no inspectable theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximity-Scaling Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling based on proximity of coarse and exact minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be integrally convex with bounded effective domain. For a power of two \(\alpha\), compute a minimizer \(x^\alpha\) of \(f\) on an appropriate translate of \(\alpha\mathbb Z^n\). The integrally convex proximity theorem ensures that some global minimizer \(x^*\) satisfies
\[
\lVert x^\alpha-x^*\rVert_\infty\le n(\alpha-1).
\]
Restrict the next finer problem to this certified box, replace \(\alpha\) by \(\alpha/2\), and repeat. At \(\alpha=1\), solve the remaining unit-scale problem and output its global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coarse-grid minimizer localizes an exact integrally convex minimizer, allowing repeated scale halving inside certified boxes.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is integrally convex with nonempty bounded effective domain.
Each coarse problem is solved on the prescribed translated lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x^*\in\arg\min f\) with \(\lVert x^\alpha-x^*\rVert_\infty\le n(\alpha-1)\), enabling exact unit-scale termination.

notation.meaning: A minimizer on the current coarse lattice.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact bound n(alpha-1) depends on the applicable integrally convex proximity theorem and the precise coarse-grid or alpha-local-optimality hypothesis. The phrase 'appropriate translate' is insufficient to validate the algorithm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain-integral L-natural-convex proximity theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided proximity from local optimality along signed subset directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be a domain-integral $L^{\natural}$-convex function on $\mathbb R^V$. Let $y\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\mathbb Z^V$ and $\alpha>0$. If $$f(y)\le f(y+\alpha\chi_X)\quad\text{and}\quad f(y)\le f(y-\alpha\chi_X)\qquad(X\subseteq V),$$ then, writing $n=|V|$, there exists $x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}f$ such that $$y-(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf 1\le x^*\le y+(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf 1.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a domain-integral L-natural-convex function, local optimality in both signed subset directions guarantees a global minimizer within the stated symmetric coordinatewise bounds.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is domain-integral and }L^{\natural}\text{-convex on }\mathbb R^V
\forall X\subseteq V:\ f(y)\le f(y+\alpha\chi_X)\text{ and }f(y)\le f(y-\alpha\chi_X)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}f:\ y-(|V|-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf 1\le x^*\le y+(|V|-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf 1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral M-Natural-Convex Proximity Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise proximity of an integral global minimizer to an integral point locally optimal for scaled M-natural exchange moves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite with \(n=|V|\), let \(\chi_0=0\), and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^{V}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a domain-integral \(M^{\natural}\)-convex function. If \(z\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) and \(\alpha>0\) satisfy \(f(z)\le f(z+\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v))\) for all \(u,v\in V\cup\{0\}\), then there exists an integral minimizer \(x^*\) satisfying \(z-n\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\le x^*\le z+n\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\) coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a domain-integral M-natural-convex function, if an integral point cannot be improved by any scaled exchange, addition, or deletion move of length alpha, then an integral global minimizer exists within coordinatewise distance n ceiling(alpha−1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\cap\mathbb{Z}^{V}:\ z-n\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\le x^*\le z+n\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-Convex Proximity Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic meaning of a proximity theorem and its M-convex scaling setting; no quantitative bound is asserted in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proximity theorem guarantees the existence of an optimal solution of an original optimization problem in a neighborhood of an optimal solution of an approximating problem. In the M-convex setting, the original problem minimizes an M-convex function $f$, while the approximation locally minimizes its positive-integer scaling $f^\alpha$. Although $f^\alpha$ need not be M-convex and a local minimizer of $f^\alpha$ need not be globally optimal for $f^\alpha$, the M-proximity theorem guarantees that some global minimizer of $f$ lies in a neighborhood of that local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximity theorem places an optimum of the original problem near an optimum of an approximation. For M-convex minimization, a global minimizer of f lies near a local minimizer of its positive-integer scaling, even though the scaled function need not be M-convex.
assumptions_latex: x^\alpha\text{ is a local minimizer of the scaling }f^\alpha
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in\arg\min f\text{ in a neighborhood of }x^\alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral M-Convex Proximity Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise proximity of an integral global minimizer to an integral point locally optimal for scaled exchange moves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite with \(n=|V|\), and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^{V}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a domain-integral \(M\)-convex function. If \(z\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) and \(\alpha>0\) satisfy \(f(z)\le f(z+\alpha(\chi_u-\chi_v))\) for all \(u,v\in V\), then \(f\) has an integral minimizer \(x^*\) satisfying \(z-(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\le x^*\le z+(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\) coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a domain-integral M-convex function, if an integral point z cannot be improved by any exchange step of length alpha, then some integral global minimizer lies within coordinatewise distance (n−1) ceiling(alpha−1) of z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\cap\mathbb{Z}^{V}:\ z-(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\le x^*\le z+(n-1)\lceil\alpha-1\rceil\mathbf{1}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-Minimizer Cut with Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise minimizer cuts derived from best alpha-scaled exchange moves for an M-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbf Z^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be M-convex with $\arg\min f\neq\varnothing$, let $\alpha\in\mathbf Z_{++}$, and let $n=|V|$. (i) Given $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $v\in V$, if $u\in V$ satisfies $f(x+\alpha(\chi_v-\chi_u))=\min_{s\in V}f(x+\alpha(\chi_v-\chi_s))$, then there exists $x^*\in\arg\min f$ such that $x^*(u)\leq x(u)-\alpha(1-\chi_v(u))+(n-1)(\alpha-1)$. (ii) Given $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $u\in V$, if $v\in V$ satisfies $f(x+\alpha(\chi_v-\chi_u))=\min_{t\in V}f(x+\alpha(\chi_t-\chi_u))$, then there exists $x^*\in\arg\min f$ such that $x^*(v)\geq x(v)+\alpha(1-\chi_u(v))-(n-1)(\alpha-1)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an M-convex function having a minimizer, a best alpha-scaled exchange yields a coordinatewise cut satisfied by some global minimizer. Selecting the best departure coordinate gives an upper cut, while selecting the best arrival coordinate gives a lower cut, with correction (n−1)(alpha−1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in\arg\min f\text{ satisfying }x^*(u)\leq x(u)-\alpha(1-\chi_v(u))+(n-1)(\alpha-1)\text{ in case (i), or }x^*(v)\geq x(v)+\alpha(1-\chi_u(v))-(n-1)(\alpha-1)\text{ in case (ii)}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled-lattice proximity in the standard L-convex, rather than L-natural-convex, formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be L-convex and attain its minimum. For \(\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), suppose \(x^{\alpha}\in\arg\min\{f(x)\mid x\in\alpha\mathbb{Z}^n\}\). Then a global minimizer \(x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n}f(x)\) can be chosen so that \[\lVert x^*-x^{\alpha}\rVert_\infty\le n(\alpha-1).\] Thus optimization on the coarse lattice localizes at least one exact minimizer to a bounded integer box around \(x^{\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coarse-lattice minimizer of an L-convex function has a global minimizer within max-distance n(alpha−1).
knowledge_statements.title: L-Convex Proximity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximity from alpha-local optimality for an integrally convex extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be integrally convex and attain its minimum. Fix \(\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) and \(x^{\alpha}\in\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(x^{\alpha}\) is alpha-locally optimal in the sense that \[f(x^{\alpha})\le f(x^{\alpha}+\alpha d)\qquad\text{for every }d\in\{-1,0,1\}^n,\] then there exists \(x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n}f(x)\) such that \[\lVert x^*-x^{\alpha}\rVert_\infty\le n(\alpha-1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alpha-local optimality for an integrally convex function places some global minimizer within max-distance n(alpha−1).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If no feasible unit exchange decreases \(f\) at \(x\), then \(x\in\arg\min f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-exchange local optimality criterion for M-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be M-convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then \(x\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) if and only if \[f(x)\le f(x-e_i+e_j)\] for every \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for which \(x-e_i+e_j\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Consequently, the absence of an improving feasible unit exchange is a complete, finitely checkable global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an M-convex function, a feasible point is globally optimal exactly when no unit exchange improves it.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Optimality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-exchange local-to-global criterion is standard and property is an acceptable kind for this structural leaf, but no inspectable DCA source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Flow Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear minimum-cost flow interface with integral data and node-potential dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\). For supplies \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^V\), costs \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^A\), and integral bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{Z}^A\) with \(\ell\le u\), the minimum-cost flow problem is \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}z\mid Bz=b,\ \ell\le z\le u\}.\] Its linear-programming dual uses node potentials \(p\in\mathbb{R}^V\) and bound multipliers \(r,s\in\mathbb{R}_+^A\): \[\max\{b^{\mathsf T}p+\ell^{\mathsf T}r-u^{\mathsf T}s\mid B^{\mathsf T}p+r-s=c\}.\] If the primal is feasible, strong linear-programming duality gives equal optimal values, and total unimodularity of \(B\) with integral \(b,\ell,u\) yields an integral optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible minimum-cost flow problem has a node-potential linear-programming dual, and integral bounds and supplies permit an integral optimal flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\).
\(b\in\mathbb{Z}^V\), \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^A\), and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{Z}^A\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\), and the flow constraints are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed primal and dual have equal optimal values, and the primal has an integral optimal solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer M-convex/M-concave Fenchel duality with explicit conjugate conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For proper functions \(f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\), define \[f^*(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\},\qquad g_*(p)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-g(x)\}.\] If \(f\) is M-convex, \(g\) is M-concave, and the relevant optima are attained, discrete Fenchel duality states \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n}\{f(x)-g(x)\}=\max_{p\in\mathbb{Z}^n}\{g_*(p)-f^*(p)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum difference of an M-convex and M-concave function equals an integer-price maximization of their discrete conjugates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-capacity function for lower- and upper-bounded flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract ends with a malformed trailing fragment, but the displayed definitions themselves are complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq V\), define \(\Delta^+X=\{a\in A\mid \partial^+a\in X,\ \partial^-a\in V\setminus X\}\) and \(\Delta^-X=\{a\in A\mid \partial^-a\in X,\ \partial^+a\in V\setminus X\}\). The cut-capacity function \(\kappa:2^V\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is \(\kappa(X)=\sum_{a\in\Delta^+X}\bar c(a)-\sum_{a\in\Delta^-X}\underline c(a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The outgoing and incoming cuts of a vertex set are defined by arc orientation. Its cut capacity is the sum of upper bounds on outgoing arcs minus the sum of lower bounds on incoming arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa(X)=\bar c(\Delta^+X)-\underline c(\Delta^-X)=\sum_{a\in\Delta^+X}\bar c(a)-\sum_{a\in\Delta^-X}\underline c(a).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut characterization and base-polyhedron representation of bounded-flow boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real feasibility and the integral refinement when both bound functions are integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar c:A\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(\underline c:A\to\mathbf R\cup\{-\infty\}\), and \(x:V\to\mathbf R\). There exists \(\xi:A\to\mathbf R\) satisfying \(\underline c(a)\leq\xi(a)\leq\bar c(a)\) for all \(a\in A\) and \(\partial\xi=x\) if and only if \(x(X)\leq\kappa(X)\) for every \(X\subseteq V\) and \(x(V)=0\). Hence \(\mathbf B(\kappa)=\{\partial\xi\mid\xi:A\to\mathbf R,\ \underline c\leq\xi\leq\bar c\}\). If \(\underline c\) and \(\bar c\) are integer-valued, then \(\mathbf B(\kappa)\cap\mathbf Z^V=\{\partial\xi\mid\xi:A\to\mathbf Z,\ \underline c\leq\xi\leq\bar c\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is the boundary of a bounded real flow exactly when it has total sum zero and satisfies every cut-capacity inequality. These boundary vectors form the base polyhedron of the cut-capacity function. With integer-valued bounds, its integral points are precisely the boundaries of bounded integer flows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\xi:A\to\mathbf R:\ [\underline c\leq\xi\leq\bar c\land\partial\xi=x]\iff[(\forall X\subseteq V)\ x(X)\leq\kappa(X)]\land[x(V)=0],\quad \mathbf B(\kappa)\cap\mathbf Z^V=\{\partial\xi\mid\xi\in\mathbf Z^A,\ \underline c\leq\xi\leq\bar c\}\text{ if }\underline c,\bar c\text{ are integer-valued}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-polyhedron representation linking separable M-convex minimization to submodular flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^V\) be an integral base polyhedron and let \(\varphi_i:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be discrete convex for each \(i\in V\). Define \[f(x)=\sum_{i\in V}\varphi_i(x_i)+\delta_{B\cap\mathbb{Z}^V}(x),\] where \(\delta_{B\cap\mathbb{Z}^V}(x)=0\) on \(B\cap\mathbb{Z}^V\) and equals \(+\infty\) otherwise. Then \(f\) is M-convex. Hence minimizing separable convex costs over integral base-polyhedron points is an M-convex minimization problem and admits the standard submodular-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separable discrete-convex minimization over an integral base polyhedron is M-convex and interfaces with submodular flow.
knowledge_statements.title: M-Convex Submodular-Flow Route

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The base-polyhedron construction plausibly defines an M-convex function, but the claimed standard submodular-flow formulation is an additional algorithmic representation requiring a precise source and scope.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equilibrium Reconstruction from an Optimal MSFP2 Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derives market clearing and agent optimality from an optimal flow and normalized optimal potential, including the nonnegative-price condition and the converse allocation assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\in\mathbf Z^A\) be an optimal flow and \(\bar p\in\mathbf R^{V^+\cup V^-}\) an optimal potential for the specified \(\mathrm{MSFP}_2\) instance, with \(\bar p(0_e^+)=0\). Define \(x_h^*=-\partial\xi|_{V_h^-\setminus\{0_h^-\}}\), \(y_l^*=\partial\xi|_{V_l^+\setminus\{0_l^+\}}\), and \(p=\bar p|_{V_e^+\setminus\{0_e^+\}}\), regarded as vectors on \(K\). Then \(x^\circ+\sum_{l\in L}y_l^*=\sum_{h\in H}x_h^*\), \(x_h^*\in\arg\max U_h[-p]\) for every \(h\in H\), and \(y_l^*\in\arg\min C_l[-p]\) for every \(l\in L\). If \(p\geq0\), the reconstructed allocations and prices form an equilibrium. Moreover, if an equilibrium exists, the reconstructed consumptions and productions are the allocations of some equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal MSFP2 flow and normalized optimal potential reconstruct market-clearing, individually optimal allocations. They form an equilibrium when the reconstructed prices are nonnegative; if any equilibrium exists, these reconstructed allocations occur in one.
assumptions_latex: \xi\in\mathbf Z^A\text{ is an optimal flow for the specified }\mathrm{MSFP}_2\text{ instance}
\bar p\in\mathbf R^{V^+\cup V^-}\text{ is an optimal potential with }\bar p(0_e^+)=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\circ+\sum_{l\in L}y_l^*=\sum_{h\in H}x_h^*,\quad x_h^*\in\arg\max U_h[-p],\quad y_l^*\in\arg\min C_l[-p];\quad p\geq0\Rightarrow((x_h^*)_{h\in H},(y_l^*)_{l\in L},p)\text{ is an equilibrium},\text{ and equilibrium existence implies that the reconstructed allocations occur in some equilibrium.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MSFP2 Algorithm for Computing Extremal-Price Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes equilibrium allocations and a largest or smallest equilibrium price vector, preserving the nonexistence outcomes at both stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct the associated \(\mathrm{MSFP}_2\) instance. Solve it to obtain \((x_h^*)_{h\in H}\), \((y_l^*)_{l\in L}\), and a potential-derived price vector; if \(\mathrm{MSFP}_2\) is infeasible, conclude that no equilibrium exists. Otherwise solve problem \((11.44)\) to obtain an equilibrium with the largest equilibrium price vector \(p^*\); if \((11.44)\) is infeasible, conclude that no equilibrium exists. Replacing \((11.44)\) by \((11.45)\) in the second stage computes the smallest equilibrium price vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the constructed MSFP2 instance for allocations, then solve the price constraint problem for the largest equilibrium price vector; use the alternate price problem for the smallest vector. Infeasibility at either stated stage implies that no equilibrium exists.
assumptions_latex: \text{The market instance admits the stated construction of }\mathrm{MSFP}_2\text{ and price problems }(11.44)\text{ and }(11.45)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{MSFP}_2\text{ infeasible}\Rightarrow\text{no equilibrium};\quad \mathrm{MSFP}_2\text{ solved and }(11.44)\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow\text{an equilibrium with the largest price vector};\quad (11.44)\text{ infeasible}\Rightarrow\text{no equilibrium};\quad (11.45)\text{ in place of }(11.44)\text{ yields the smallest price vector.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-Natural Convexity and Extremal Equilibrium Prices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure of the complete equilibrium-price set under M-natural-concave utilities, M-natural-convex costs, and equilibrium existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that every utility function \(U_h\) (\(h\in H\)) is \(M^
atural\)-concave, every cost function \(C_l\) (\(l\in L\)) is \(M^
atural\)-convex, and an equilibrium exists for the total initial endowment \(x^\circ\). Then the set \(P^*(x^\circ)\) of all equilibrium price vectors is an \(L^

children.title: Gross-Substitutes Valuations
children.top_down_role: Local connective material for gross-substitutes valuation structure.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite item set and \(v:2^E\to\mathbb{R}\) is a valuation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gross substitutes means unchanged-price items in an old demanded bundle can be retained in some new demanded bundle after prices rise.

notation.meaning: sum of item prices over X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kelso–Crawford demand formulation for indivisible, unit-demanded copies of items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite item set \(E\), define \(p(X)=\sum_{j\in X}p_j\) and \[D_v(p)=\arg\max_{X\subseteq E}\{v(X)-p(X)\}.\] The valuation \(v:2^E\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies gross substitutes if, for every \(p,q\in\mathbb{R}^E\) with \(p\le q\) and every \(X\in D_v(p)\), there exists \(Y\in D_v(q)\) such that \[\{j\in X\mid p_j=q_j\}\subseteq Y.\] Thus goods demanded before the price increase whose own prices remain fixed can simultaneously remain demanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valuation is gross substitutes when unchanged-price goods from any old demanded bundle can remain in some bundle demanded after prices rise.
knowledge_statements.title: Gross-Substitutes Valuations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The demand-based definition is precise and fits the definition leaf, but gross substitutes has several equivalent formulations and this exact Kelso–Crawford variant lacks a citation.

children.title: Market Equilibrium Interface
children.top_down_role: Local connective material for equilibrium models linked to discrete convexity.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many agents and finitely many indivisible goods, each with unit supply.
Every agent has a gross-substitutes valuation and quasilinear utility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A Walrasian equilibrium exists, and every equilibrium allocation maximizes total valuation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Walrasian existence for unit-supply indivisible goods under gross-substitutes valuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider finitely many agents and a finite set \(E\) of indivisible goods with unit supplies. Suppose every agent \(i\) has a gross-substitutes valuation \(v_i:2^E\to\mathbb{R}\) and utility \(v_i(X)-p(X)\). Then there exist pairwise disjoint bundles \((X_i)_i\) and prices \(p\in\mathbb{R}_+^E\) such that \(X_i\in D_{v_i}(p)\) for every \(i\), and every unallocated good has price zero. Moreover, any such Walrasian allocation solves \[\max\left\{\sum_i v_i(X_i)\mid X_i\subseteq E,\ X_i\cap X_j=\varnothing\text{ for }i\ne j\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gross-substitutes valuations guarantee Walrasian prices and a welfare-maximizing allocation of unit-supply indivisible goods.
knowledge_statements.title: Market Equilibrium Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the market-equilibrium interface, but existence with nonnegative prices and the zero-price convention for unallocated goods requires a source specifying normalization, monotonicity, and free-disposal conventions.

children.title: Demand–Price Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The structural connection between gross-substitutes demand plus equilibrium prices.

assumptions_latex: Agent \(i\) has demand correspondence \(D_i(p)\) at price \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Price \(p\) clears the market exactly when \(s\in\sum_i\{\mathbf{1}_X\mid X\in D_i(p)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued demand characterization of market-clearing prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each agent \(i\), let \(D_i(p)\) be the bundles maximizing quasilinear utility at price \(p\), and let \(s\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E\) be aggregate supply. The price vector \(p\) supports a market-clearing selection precisely when \[s\in\sum_i\{\mathbf{1}_X\mid X\in D_i(p)\},\] where the sum is a Minkowski sum. Equivalently, there are bundles \(X_i\in D_i(p)\) satisfying \(\sum_i\mathbf{1}_{X_i}=s\). Thus demanded bundles together with their incidence vectors provide a directly verifiable equilibrium certificate at \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prices clear the market exactly when demanded-bundle incidence vectors can be selected to sum to the supply vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand–Price Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The incidence-vector equality is a valid certificate for exact clearing, but it is not equivalent to equilibrium under conventions allowing unsold zero-price goods. A source must fix the intended clearing convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Boundary of Convex Extendability on the Integer Lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The temporary extendability definition behaves adequately in one dimension but is too weak to guarantee discrete separation in higher dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Temporarily call f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{+\infty\} convex when there exists a convex \bar f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} satisfying \bar f(x)=f(x) for every x\in\mathbb{Z}^n. When n=1, this condition is equivalent to \[f(x-1)+f(x+1)\ge 2f(x)\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}),\] and the associated one-dimensional discrete separation and Fenchel-duality statements hold. In higher dimensions, convex extendability alone does not ensure discrete separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lattice convexity defined only through extension to a real convex function is equivalent in one dimension to nonnegative second differences and supports the stated one-dimensional separation and duality results. In higher dimensions, that definition is insufficient to guarantee discrete separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n=1\Rightarrow\left[\text{convex extendability}\iff f(x-1)+f(x+1)\ge 2f(x)\ \forall x\in\mathbb{Z}\right];\quad n>1:\ \text{convex extendability alone need not imply discrete separation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Separation Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The precise discrete convexity and concavity classes are not specified in the extract and are essential hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{+\infty\} and h:\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty\} be respectively convex and concave in an appropriate discrete sense. If f(x)\ge h(x) for every x\in\mathbb{Z}^n, then there exist \alpha^*\in\mathbb{Z} and p^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n such that \[f(x)\ge \alpha^*+\langle p^*,x\rangle\ge h(x)\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an appropriately discrete-convex function dominates an appropriately discrete-concave function everywhere on the integer lattice, an integral affine function lies between them everywhere.

children.title: Exchange-Structure Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of exchange-based discrete convex structure.

assumptions_latex: Extended-real-valued functions use \(+\infty\) to exclude points from their effective domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bounded constant-sum domain need not satisfy the M-convex exchange axiom.

notation.meaning: the ith unit vector in four dimensions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete constant-sum domain violating every required exchange between its two points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{Z}^4\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \(f(1,1,0,0)=f(0,0,1,1)=0\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Put \(x=(1,1,0,0)\) and \(y=(0,0,1,1)\). For \(i=1\), the M-convex exchange axiom would require some \(j\in\{3,4\}\) with both \(x-e_1+e_j\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(y+e_1-e_j\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Neither choice satisfies even the first membership condition. Hence \(f\) is not M-convex, although its domain is finite and all domain points have coordinate sum two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two isolated equal-cardinality incidence vectors form a bounded constant-sum domain but violate the M-convex exchange axiom.

assumptions_latex: Discrete midpoint convexity is tested for all \(x,y\in D\) with \(|x-y|\ge 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The discrete midpoint inequality fails for \(x=0\) and \(y=2\).

notation.meaning: Extended-real-valued function on the integer line.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional failure of discrete midpoint convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=f(2)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\). Discrete midpoint convexity would require
\[
f(x)+f(y)\ge f\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+f\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rceil\right)
\]
whenever the two midpoint arguments belong to \(D\). For \(x=0\) and \(y=2\), this becomes \(0+0\ge 1+1\), which is false. Thus an integer-domain function need not possess discrete midpoint structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function with endpoint values zero and midpoint value one violates the discrete midpoint inequality at the pair 0 and 2.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Structural Survival
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-midpoint closure can survive after the constant-sum M-convex exchange property is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(0,0),(1,0),(2,0)\}\subset\mathbb Z^2\). For every \(x,y\in S\), the componentwise points \(\lfloor(x+y)/2\rfloor\) and \(\lceil(x+y)/2\rceil\) belong to \(S\), so \(S\) is discrete-midpoint closed. The constant-sum M-convex exchange axiom would require that, whenever \(x_i>y_i\), there exist a coordinate \(j\) with \(x_j<y_j\) such that \(x-e_i+e_j\in S\) and \(y+e_i-e_j\in S\). For \(x=(2,0)\), \(y=(0,0)\), and \(i=1\), no coordinate \(j\) satisfies \(x_j<y_j\). Hence \(S\) fails this exchange axiom while retaining discrete-midpoint closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-point lattice segment is closed under floor-ceiling midpoints but fails the constant-sum M-convex exchange axiom because the required compensating coordinate does not exist.
assumptions_latex: Midpoint closure uses componentwise floor and ceiling.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S\) is discrete-midpoint closed but does not satisfy the constant-sum M-convex exchange axiom.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=0\), \(f(1)=2\), and \(f(2)=1\), and let \(N_D(x)=\{y\in D:|x-y|=1\}\). Since \(N_D(2)=\{1\}\) and \(f(2)=1\le f(1)=2\), the point \(2\) is a local minimizer. Nevertheless, \(f(0)=0<f(2)=1\), so \(2\) is not globally minimizing. Hence unit-neighborhood local optimality alone does not certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a three-point domain, the endpoint 2 beats its only neighbor but is worse than the distant feasible point 0.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Minima without Global Certification

assumptions_latex: Variables in the primal integer problem satisfy \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
The relaxation replaces integrality by \(x_i\ge0\) while retaining the triangle edge inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer optimum is \(1\), whereas the primal and dual linear-programming optima are \(3/2\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual variables indexed by triangle edges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Triangle stable set exhibits an integrality gap despite linear-programming duality.

source_refs.locator: Linear Programming and Duality p. 14

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the triangle, consider
\[
\max\{x_1+x_2+x_3:x_i+x_j\le1\ \text{for all edges }ij,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\}.
\]
Its optimum is \(1\). In the linear relaxation, \(x_1=x_2=x_3=1/2\) is feasible with value \(3/2\). The dual relaxation is
\[
\min\{y_{12}+y_{23}+y_{31}:y_{12}+y_{31}\ge1,\ y_{12}+y_{23}\ge1,\ y_{23}+y_{31}\ge1,\ y\ge0\},
\]
and \(y_{12}=y_{23}=y_{31}=1/2\) is optimal. Thus primal-dual equality survives over the reals, but an integral primal-dual optimum does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The triangle stable-set formulation has integer optimum one but fractional primal and dual optima three halves, so integral duality is lost.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Integral Duality

assumptions_latex: Discrete midpoint convexity on \(\mathbb Z\) uses the floor-ceiling midpoint inequality.
Both component functions are finite-valued on \(\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise minimum \(h=\min\{f_1,f_2\}\) is not discrete midpoint convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convexity of the quadratics and failure of their minimum follow by direct substitution
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise minimum does not preserve discrete midpoint convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(t)=t^2\) and \(f_2(t)=(t-2)^2\) for \(t\in\mathbb Z\). Each satisfies the one-dimensional discrete midpoint inequality and is therefore discrete midpoint convex. Define \(h(t)=\min\{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}\). Then \(h(0)=0\), \(h(1)=1\), and \(h(2)=0\). Applied to \(x=0\) and \(y=2\), discrete midpoint convexity would require \(h(0)+h(2)\ge2h(1)\), namely \(0\ge2\). Thus this discrete-convex class is not closed under pointwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of two shifted convex quadratics fails the midpoint inequality, showing nonclosure under pointwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosure under Discrete-Convex Operations

children.title: Dimensional Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Limitations driven by ambient or effective dimension.

assumptions_latex: The domain is the integer box \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n\{L_i,\ldots,U_i\}\).
An exhaustive method evaluates the objective once at every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive evaluation requires \(\prod_{i=1}^n(U_i-L_i+1)\) oracle calls, which can be exponential in \(n\).

notation.meaning: Integer box serving as the feasible domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension alone makes direct enumeration exponential on bounded-width boxes.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Complexity Theory: P and NP p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The box cardinality is
\[
|B|=\prod_{i=1}^n(U_i-L_i+1).
\]
Consequently, an exhaustive value-oracle minimization method makes exactly \(|B|\) objective evaluations in the worst case before certifying the minimum. In particular, if every coordinate has only two admissible values, so that \(U_i-L_i+1=2\), then \(|B|=2^n\). Thus bounded coordinate width does not prevent an exponential dependence on the dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating an integer box costs the product of its coordinate widths and already requires two to the n evaluations for binary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimensional Bottlenecks

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Complexity Theory: P and NP p. 21

children.title: Domain-Geometry Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Limitations driven by irregular, sparse, or constrained domains.

assumptions_latex: Feasible moves are unit coordinate steps that remain in the domain.
Local optimality compares an objective value only with values at feasible moves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disconnected unit-step geometry permits a nonglobal point to satisfy every local optimality test.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the geometric obstruction and objective comparison are directly checkable
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected feasible geometry destroys unit-neighborhood certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{0,2\}\subset\mathbb Z\), and connect two feasible points only when their distance is \(1\). The induced feasible-neighbor graph has no edges. Define \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(2)=1\). Because \(2\) has no feasible unit-step neighbor, the inequalities \(f(2)\le f(y)\) for all feasible neighbors \(y\) hold vacuously. Yet \(f(0)<f(2)\). Therefore local certification requires suitable domain geometry, such as connectivity by admissible moves, in addition to objective comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a unit-step-disconnected domain, a worse isolated point is vacuously locally optimal, so domain geometry blocks local-to-global reasoning.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Geometry Bottlenecks

children.title: Encoding-Size Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Limitations driven by input representation size.

assumptions_latex: The upper bound \(U\ge1\) is encoded in binary.
An exhaustive method evaluates every integer in \(D=\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumeration uses \(U+1\) evaluations, exponential in the binary encoding length \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the interval cardinality.
Integer interval serving as the domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional interval may be exponentially large relative to its binary description.

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The domain has \(|D|=U+1\) feasible points, while its upper endpoint requires only \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\) bits up to a constant-size encoding convention. Hence exhaustive value-oracle minimization makes \(U+1\) evaluations, and
\[
2^{\ell-1}<U+1\le2^\ell.
\]
The enumeration cost is therefore exponential in \(\ell\), even though the dimension is fixed at one. Polynomial dependence on numerical magnitude is only pseudopolynomial when bounds are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary-encoded one-dimensional interval contains exponentially many points relative to the number of bits describing its endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Size Bottlenecks

children.title: Combined Input-Regime Barriers
children.top_down_role: Interactions among dimension, domain geometry, plus encoding scale.

assumptions_latex: The domain is \(B=\{0,1,\ldots,U\}^n\) with \(U\ge1\) encoded in binary.
The algorithm exhaustively evaluates every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method uses \((U+1)^n=2^{n\log_2(U+1)}\) evaluations, combining dimensional and numerical-magnitude growth.

notation.meaning: Integer box serving as the feasible domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension and binary coordinate range multiply into a joint enumeration barrier.

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23
Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The box contains
\[
|B|=(U+1)^n=2^{n\log_2(U+1)}
\]
feasible points. An exhaustive value-oracle method therefore requires exactly \((U+1)^n\) evaluations in the worst case. This cost is exponential in \(n\) when \(U\) is fixed above zero and exponential in the binary length of \(U\) when \(n\) is fixed above zero. Thus simultaneous growth of dimension and coordinate range compounds rather than separates the two enumeration bottlenecks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An n-dimensional binary-encoded box has size equal to its coordinate range raised to n, combining both input-regime bottlenecks.
knowledge_statements.title: Combined Input-Regime Barriers
